ARTICLE IN PRESS Fostering tolerance through museums: assessing visitor engagement with historical analogies at three archaeological galleries in the UK Authors: Dr Chiara Bonacchi,* chiara.bonacchi@ed.ac.uk, School of History, Classics and Archaeology, University of Edinburgh, UK Dr Marta Krzyzanska, m.krzyzanska@sheffield.ac.uk, School of Mathematical and Physical Sciences, University of Sheffield, UK Dr Kate Sharpe, kate.sharpe@durham.ac.uk, Department of Archaeology, Durham University, S UK S Dr Zachary Horne, zachary.horne@ed.ac.uk, School of PhiElosophy, Psychology and Language Sciences, University of Edinburgh, UK R P Professor Richard Hingley, richard.hingley@durham.ac.uk, Department of Archaeology, Durham University, UK N I * Corresponding author E L C I Abstract T R This study is the first to quantitatively investigate museum visitors' perceptions of historical A analogies that compare concepts from the deep past with modern political ideas. Specifically, we assess the capacity of heritage sites to influence visitors’ historical consciousness in ways that foster tolerance by exposing and challenging those analogies that feature in exclusive nationalist discourse. This is achieved by analysing the responses submitted by 803 visitors who engaged with the Tolerant Futures interactive, which was displayed in the archaeological galleries of three UK museums. Our findings show that visitors' views did not align with the positions implied by the historical analogies used in exclusive nationalist discourse. By contrast, most participants held critical and non-binary understandings of the Iron Age and Roman past, as well as liberal values. We conclude that museums have a limited ability to attract adults with authoritarian views and to alter their beliefs. However, we propose that they could play a crucial role in activating intergenerational attitude change and tolerance through programmes aimed at promoting nuanced and non-binary interpretations of the ancient past among children. These results are significant for researchers and practitioners in heritage, museum studies, cultural sociology, psychology and cultural policy. Keywords: tolerance, historical analogies, heritage, museum visitors, Bayesian modelling, political attitudes, attitude change ARTICLE IN PRESS 1. Introduction Recent years have seen an increase in explicitly activist agendas in archaeology, history, heritage and museums. Researchers in these fields have advocated the need to expose and challenge socially exclusive uses of the past (Rosenzweig, 2020) that feature in racist or populist nationalist discourse (Gardner, 2017; Hanscam, 2019; Flewellen et al., 2021). They have emphasised the importance of communicating more accurately and persuasively to pre-empt or counter exaggerated and stereotypical views of the past that are leveraged to antagonise specific groups today (Richardson and Booth, 2017; Brophy, 2018; Bonacchi, 2022). In a much-debated commentary, González-Ruibal and colleagues (2018: 507) argue that the multivocal model adopted by archaeologists, anthropologists and heritage workers in previous decades has effectively disempowered them. The solution proposed by the authors to combat authoritarianism–understood as an attempt ‘to restore an earlier state of society, driven by nostalgia or perceived loss’–is an ‘archaeology that provokes the People [...] and embraces education’ (González-Ruibal, González, and Criado-Boado, 2018S: 511). S Archaeologists, historians and heritage professionals have highlighted museums as key spaces E for implementing educational interventions focused on promoting inclusivity (Apayidin, 2022; R Bonacchi, 2022). At the same time, museum studies scholarship has reflected on museums’ P ability to ‘counter prejudice by reframing, informing and enabling society’s conversations about difference’ (Sandell, 2006: 173; Adams, 2017; Schorch et al., 2015; Bowers et al., 2015). These N discussions have intersected with the growing debate regarding the need to broaden museum I audiences beyond liberal visitors (Gurian, 2017; Message, 2022). In this context, initial empirical research has qualitatively investigated thEe relationship between people’s political attitudes and their responses to historical museum dLisplays (Bozoglu, 2019). However, no published work has yet quantitatively examined correlCations between museum visitors’ political values and their beliefs about aspects of the deepI past that are frequently weaponised by parties and politicians, even though antiquity plays aT central role in historical analogies that are widespread in political and public discourse (e.g.R, Bonacchi, Altaweel, and Krzyzanska, 2018; Barclay and Brophy, 2021; Bonacchi, 2022;A Farrell-Banks, 2023). Our study addresses this research problem by focusing on museums–understood as heritage sites or ‘theatres of memory and places of heritage-making’ (Smith, 2021: 2)–that display archaeological collections relating to the ancient human past, and the conclusions we reach can be extended to other sites that fit this definition. In particular, the article assesses the effectiveness of on-site interventions for creating tolerant futures by challenging historical analogies that feature in exclusive nationalist discourse and are underpinned by binary views of the Iron Age and Roman (IAR) past, linked to binary views of present-day concepts. This goal is achieved through the analysis of responses collected from 803 visitors who interacted with the Tolerant Futures intervention at three museums in the UK (see section 4, Methods). Data distributions and predictive modelling shed light on the research aim by allowing us to answer three empirical questions: RQ1. What are the political values and ideologies of those engaged through the intervention? RQ2. What views of the IAR past do they hold and how binary are they? RQ3. Do their views of the IAR past predict their attitudes towards contemporary politics? ARTICLE IN PRESS More specifically, through RQ1 and RQ2 we evaluate the extent to which the case study museums can engage the target audience–namely, individuals whose attitudes towards the IAR past and the present align with positions implied by historical analogies commonly leveraged to justify divisive nationalist sentiment. RQ3 assesses whether views of the IAR past predict present-day political attitudes and, by extension, whether influencing visitors’ historical consciousness by challenging specific historical analogies may foster tolerance. The next section situates these questions and explains their relevance in the context of existing literature. First, we discuss the growing attention to the activist role of museums and their work towards social inclusion, highlighting gaps in evaluating visitors’ political ideas and interventions aimed at promoting tolerance. Second, we present the theoretical lens we use to bridge these gaps. 2. Background to the work S 2.1. Museums, activism and social inclusion S E With the emergence of the ‘New Museology’ movement in the 1980s (Mayrand, 1985), R museums affirmed their commitment to communities, concentrating more decisively on people P and their needs alongside the care of collections (Merriman, 1991: 1; McCall and Gray, 2014). Since then, researchers have explored ways to widen, deepen and measure museum participation. N They have investigated how differences are crafted and negotiated in museum spaces and how I diversity, understood as the co-existence of differences, can be curated and encouraged (Macdonald, 2022). Recently, some haveE reframed this focus on social inclusion as ‘social activism’, highlighting museums’ roleL in promoting social justice (Janes and Sandell, 2019). The appropriateness and scope of museCum activism have been widely debated, including in discussions about ICOM’s 2022I definition of museums, which foregrounds goals for these institutions to be ‘accessible Tand inclusive’ and to ‘foster diversity and sustainability’ (ICOM, 2022)–aims that have beeRn reinforced in recent sector reports, notably by the Museums Association (2024: 3, 8A) in the UK and the American Alliance of Museums (2023). Researchers have also specifically considered how museums should position themselves in relation to audiences who hold right-wing, authoritarian or populist attitudes (Gurian, 2017; Message, 2022; Niklasson, 2023: 17; Leser, Bareither, and Macdonald, 2024). In her battle against the politics of hate, Message (2022) asks whether museums have a duty to engage with ‘a broad spectrum of political participation’, including white supremacist voices. Message (2022) argues that hostility functions through antagonism and introduces a tension between preserving freedom of speech, on the one hand, and curbing exclusion and discrimination, on the other. In her view, this dilemma makes it very difficult for museums to dialogue with extremists such as far-right sympathisers. Conversely, Gurian (2017) has advocated welcoming visitors with opposing political views to ‘rehabilitate our democracy’. This entails inviting in all those who profoundly disagree with ‘us’, where ‘us’ refers to museum professionals–assumed to be mostly educated and liberal (Gurian, 2017). While recognising the importance of public statements and exhibitions as outright tools of resistance, Gurian (2017: 174–176) urges colleagues not to prioritise these strategies against authoritarianism but, instead, to opt for empathy. ARTICLE IN PRESS The attention to inclusivity, diversity and social justice is grounded in decades of studies showing that wealthier, highly educated and white individuals are generally over-represented among museum audiences. Merriman’s 1989 survey found that 79% of the British population took an interest in the past, but older people and those with lower socio-economic status and formal education were least likely to visit museums (Merriman, 1991: 22, 51). Subsequent research (Black, 2012; Bonacchi, 2014; Smith, 2021: 142) confirmed that museum-goers tend to have a university degree not only in Britain but also in Italy, Australia and North America (on Italy, see also La Regina, 2009). A large-scale survey undertaken by Rosenzweig and Thelen (1998) in the United States investigated how ‘Americans value, use and experience’ the pasts of their family, their racial or ethnic group, their community and the United States (Rosenzweig and Thelen, 1998: 214). They found higher education to be the main predictor of visiting history museums, whereas income was not a significant variable in this case (Rosenzweig and Thelen, 1998: 28). Building on Bourdieu (1984), researchers have also recently re-assessed how cultural capital operates in relation to intersections of class, gender and ethnicity in fields comprising visual art galleries, museums and heritage (Bennett et al., 2009, 2S021). These works further support the finding that a significantly higher percentage of art gallery and museum visitors in S Britain have degrees (Bennett et al., 2009: 123). Moreover, they reveal that class, education, age E and place of residence influence engagement with heritage in Australia, with public and R authorised heritage being most consumed by ‘the highly educated, occupying higher class P positions’ (Waterton and Gayo, 2021: 81). N None of these nationwide surveys has specifically measured the relationship between political I views–on a spectrum from liberal to conservative–and engagement with heritage and museums. However, several studies have evaluatedE audiences’ responses to museum displays addressing themes of pressing social and politicaLl significance that are relevant to diversity. For example, Smith (2021: 87–89) conducted reCsearch with heritage site visitors in the UK (in 2004 and 2007), as well as in the US and AustralIia (between 2010 and 2013). Her work showed that visitors from dominant ethnic backgroundsT were less numerous at dissonant heritage sites than at national ones; they also had a less Ractive register of engagement than visitors from non-dominant ethnic backgrounds ‘regardleAss of the type or genre of the site being visited’ (Smith, 2021: 165). Furthermore, most respondents claimed that their museum visit had not changed ‘their views about the past or the present’, but, for 20% of them, it had reinforced pre-existing opinions (Smith, 2021: 135–136). These findings are consistent with previous studies by the Smithsonian Institution, which revealed that most museum experiences tend to consolidate the beliefs, knowledge, and expectations that visitors bring with them on entry (Doering and Pekarik, 1996; Pekarik, Doering, and Karns, 1999; Pekarik and Schreiber, 2012). Such alignment between individuals’ profiles and the topics they feel comfortable with and attuned to suggests that museums may have limited capacity to provoke and trigger attitude change due to the well- known psychological phenomenon of confirmation bias (Nickerson, 1998). However, the results of other evaluations complicate this picture, providing more nuanced evidence of people’s mindsets and motivations when visiting museums that display difficult heritage. For example, Macdonald’s ethnography at the Nazi Party Rally Grounds in Nuremberg, Germany, identified a wide array of reasons for visiting this place (Macdonald, 2009). Her conclusions emphasise that ‘not all visitors were there of their own accord’ (Macdonald, 2009: 170), nor did they all share similar views on the historical and contemporary meanings of this ARTICLE IN PRESS heritage site. Likewise, in her extensive analysis of perceptions of an exhibition on German colonialism at the German Historical Museum, Merrow (2023: 118–19) reported that respondents’ feedback indicated polarised opinions. The exhibition was not visited exclusively by individuals with post-colonial or anti-colonial views. Instead, the evaluation evidenced a ‘divided public perception of the need for colonial remembrance in present-day Germany’ (Merrow, 2023: 122). Bozoglu’s qualitative research at the Panorama 1453 Museum, in Istanbul, and the Atatürk and Independence War Museum, in Ankara, has produced results that are in part consistent with Macdonald’s and Merrow’s key findings (Bozoglu, 2020). Visitors to these Ottoman-period displays tended to have political views in line with the messages conveyed by the museums and had travelled to them with clear expectations about the narratives they would encounter (Bozoglu, 2020). However, some had more intricate and composite political and religious identities that did not perfectly match or oppose the themes advocated by the museums (Bozoglu, 2020: 114–115). This ‘tripartite structure of audience positions or readings’ is also discussed in Sandell (2007: 80–81), who highlights that visitors’ responses to exhibits are not always confirmatory (although he finds that most are), but can alsSo be oppositional or negotiated, particularly when they ‘contain contradictory elements’. In sum, therefore, a quantitative study is S needed to evaluate whether museums have the ability to attract and engage audiences with E authoritarian and exclusive nationalist views, and, if so, the extent to which they can influence R their historical consciousness to promote tolerance. P 2.2. Historical consciousness and historical analogies N I In reflecting on the links between visitors’ perceptions of the present and the past, some of the museum evaluations discussed above levEerage the notion of historical consciousness (see Merriman, 1991: 31; Macdonald, 200L9). As argued by Clark and Grever (2018: 177), building on Rüsen’s work (2004), historical coCnsciousness ‘comprises the connection between past, present, and future prospects’, and is expIressed when ‘people interpret current events from the past in order to act appropriately witTh a view to the future’. Studying historical consciousness is therefore key to understanRding how political arguments are framed (e.g., Bonacchi, 2022). A Historical analogies play a crucial role in historical consciousness, as they help people to reason about the present based on existing knowledge of the past (Liu and Hilton, 2005; Hilton and Liu, 2017). Defined as ‘the process of drawing parallels between a past event and a current situation’, such analogies are ‘common in political and public discourses’ (Ghilani et al., 2017: 275). They anchor a less familiar current event (target) in a more familiar past event (source) based on certain traits–or correspondences–that the target is seen as sharing with the source (Spellman and Holyoak, 1992: 913). Historical analogies also assign ‘social roles to the actors involved’, such as heroes and villains, as well as relationships between them (Ghilani et al., 2017: 279). Thus, the salience of a historical analogy can predict the prevalence of specific attitudes towards contemporary policy and decision-making (Spellman and Holyoak, 1992). Research has shown that historical analogies are often used to articulate exclusive nationalist positions by comparing exaggerated and binary ideas–dualities–of the past and present (Hingley, Bonacchi, and Sharpe, 2018; Bozoglu, 2020; Barclay and Brophy, 2021; Bonacchi, 2022). The term ‘insistent duality’ was originally coined by Mary Beard and John Henderson (1995: 47) to refer to the recurring oppositions in perceiving the Roman period, in relation to contemporary ARTICLE IN PRESS identity, as either native or foreign, a moment of civilisation on ‘our shores’ or an ignominious case of conquest and occupation. However, these dichotomies are not limited to the Roman world. Prehistoric, Roman and post-Roman periods are, in fact, often contrasted based on how people ‘score’ them on a continuum between abstract concepts such as civilisation and barbarism, freedom and domination, being peaceful or violent, and so on (Hingley, Bonacchi, and Sharpe, 2018). Insistent dualities are widespread in populist and nationalist discourse on social media, where users describe aspects of the prehistoric, Roman and medieval past in highly polarised ways (Bonacchi, Altaweel, and Krzyzanska, 2018; Bonacchi and Krzyzanska, 2021; Bonacchi, 2022). Nationalism today defines ‘a collective inside against an outside and proclaim[s] pride in and the need to defend “our economy”, “our country” and “our way of life”’ (Fuchs, 2018: 42). It is connected with neoliberalism, globalisation and its tension with localisms, the resurgence of regional identities and an increasing rejection of supranational ones (Gardner, 2017; Fuchs, 2018). As such, contemporary nationalism is ultimately based on San ‘exclusive’ idea of nation (Delanty, 2017) while displaying global reach and interconnections as a phenomenon. In this S context, dualities about the IAR past are used to justify the exclusion of out-groups through E historical analogies, which express antagonistic ideas of specific ‘others’ perceived as enemies R (De Cesari and Kaya, 2020; Bonacchi, 2022; Farrell-Banks, 2023; Niklasson, 2023). P N 3. The Tolerant Futures interactive I Interactivity, openness of design and theE creation of encounters with others’ views were key aspects of the Tolerant Futures intervLention. This was developed to promote tolerance by exposing historical analogies that Ccompare binary ideas about the IAR past with modern or contemporary political conceptsI. Here, tolerance is understood as a three-dimensional construct, entailing the ‘acceptance of, rTespect for and appreciation of difference’ (Hjerm et al., 2019). Philosophical literature haRs shown the potential value of encountering views radically different from one’s own. MediAna (2013) introduces the concept of resistant imaginations to highlight how exposure to opposing ideas can lead someone to challenge or exercise their personal resistances. For him, preventive justice works ‘to maintain live and fluid the interplay of resistances and the epistemic friction of heterogeneous imaginations’ (Medina, 2013: 257). This way of conceptualising the negotiation of different values goes beyond discussions of antagonism and its ‘domestication’ into agonism (Medina, 2013: 276; Mouffe, 2000) and embraces ‘radical openness to difference’. Furthermore, the social psychology literature has provided evidence that intergroup contact can help to overcome confirmation bias and reduce prejudice in individuals prone to it, although the degree varies depending on the antagonised out-group and the perceived threat (Zhang, 2019; Maunder, Day, and White, 2020). Intergroup contact can occur through direct interaction with individuals or–in an ‘extended’ form–with representations of those individuals (see, e.g., the discussion in Husnu, Mertan, and Cicek, 2018). The web-based interactive Tolerant Futures was developed in line with this extended intergroup contact approach. The design of the interactive was inspired by the idea of cards that users could play with to explore concepts from the past that are rich in symbolism and strongly associated with concepts ARTICLE IN PRESS from the present. The interactive was subdivided into sections called ‘chapters’. In each chapter, users were given a card and asked to place it on a spectrum represented as a line connecting two adjectives expressing opposite meanings, or binaries. The first chapter focused on the self in the ‘Here and now’, asking users to place a card called ‘Your age’ at any point on a spectrum from ‘young’ to ‘old’; then to place a ‘Your home’ card on a spectrum from ‘near’ to ‘far’; and to place a ‘Your relationship with time’ card on a spectrum from ‘past-oriented’ to ‘future- oriented’. The purpose was to familiarise users with the functionality of the interactive before they moved on to Chapter 2. [insert Figure 1 here] The second chapter was centred on ‘The past and the present’. It explained that people sometimes connect concepts from the IAR past and from the present based on supposedly shared qualities. Users were then asked to describe concepts that are often associated with one another by placing them on a continuum between two opposite adjectivesS (Figure 1). For example, a user might be asked to place the ‘Suffragette’ card on a spectrum from benevolent to malevolent, and S then do the same with the ‘Boudica’ card. This is because the Suffragettes have been compared E to Boudica in rather dichotomous ways, either as symbols of positive progress and freedom R fighters, or as expressions of ‘difficult women’ identities. Users could also add a sentence to P explain why they placed a given IAR-related card where they did. The concepts and spectra used in the interactive are listed in Tables 1 and 2. They were derived from research on the uses of N Iron Age and Roman heritage, especially in modern history (Hingley, 2001; Hingley and Unwin, I 2005; Gillespie, 2018) and contemporary populist nationalist discourse (Bonacchi, Altaweel, and Krzyzanska, 2018; Hingley, Bonacchi, aEnd Sharpe, 2018; Bonacchi, 2022). Methods I The Tolerant Futures interactive was deEsigned to save participants’ responses in a database for later analysis. The displays, with iPadLs allowing access to the Tolerant Futures web-based application, were installed in JuneC 2022 in the Roman archaeology galleries of the three case study museums and were removIed at the end of May 2023. During this twelve-month period, we collected responses from 2,56T7 individuals who interacted with Chapter 2. However, the analysis in this article focuses, conRservatively, on submissions from the 803 individuals who provided reasons for their descriAptions of concepts from the Iron Age or Roman past. This approach ensured that only pondered answers were included in the dataset. It should be noted that each visitor could engage with more than one historical analogy in Chapter 2, which explains why almost twice as many responses were submitted for Chapter 2 as there were respondents. To answer the first two research questions, we created box plots showing the distribution of scores assigned by users to concepts from the IAR past and concepts from modern history and the present. Scores were on a continuum from 0 (corresponding to the adjective at the left-hand end of the spectrum, on the interactive screen) to 1 (corresponding to the adjective at the opposite end of the spectrum, on the same interactive screen). To address the third question, we constructed a beta regression model in a Bayesian framework. This model predicts the score that a visitor assigns to the concept from modern history or the present, as a function of the interaction between the score the same visitor assigns to the concept from the IAR past they are presented with, and the pair of past–present concepts considered (e.g., Boudica–suffragettes, or European Union–Roman Empire). Different pairs of concepts from the IAR past and subsequent periods were treated by the model as different categories within the categorical variable ‘concept’. A beta regression was chosen to model the dependent variable for two reasons. Firstly, it limits the distribution to the continuous values bounded between 0 and 1, which mirrors the ARTICLE IN PRESS constraints imposed on the scores assigned by the visitors in the Tolerant Futures interactive. Secondly, a beta regression is highly flexible in terms of shape. It can be symmetrical or asymmetrical and unimodal or bimodal, depending on the predicted parameter values. Thus, it allows for distributions of scores that can represent views either clustering towards two opposite extremes or centred around one value. In the next section, we present the study findings to answer each of the three research questions in turn. 5. Results 5.1. Political values underpinned by perceptions of the modern and contemporary world (RQ1) Starting with concepts presented to users before the Boudica ‘card’ (Figure 2), the Suffragettes, the protagonists of first-wave feminism, were consistently described in very positive terms: benevolent, celebrated, civilised, dominant, heroic, regenerating, refined, progressive and reassuring. By contrast, attitudes towards two conservative political leaders, Margaret Thatcher and Theresa May, were negative overall. May, the first Prime Minister to lead the negotiations over Brexit from 2016 to 2019, was seen as very exclusive, condemned, dividing, insecure and worrying. Margaret Thatcher, the leader of the Tory party who led the United Kingdom from ARTICLE IN PRESS 1979 to 1990, championing economic liberalisation among other policies, was characterised as very incompetent, worrying, violent, non-multicultural, malevolent and condemned. [Insert Figure 2 here] Among the concepts from the present frequently associated with the Roman Empire (Figure 2), the European Union was perceived by users as very benevolent, celebrated and civilised, and as very progressive, practical, peaceful, multicultural and long-lasting. The British Empire was deemed moderately to very malevolent, condemned to varying degrees, very connecting and dominant, exclusive, non-multicultural, incompetent, insecure, very symbolic, and violent. Views on both the USSR and Nazi Germany were decidedly more negative. In comparison, users expressed more moderate and mixed P views about Jean-Claude Juncker, the Luxembourgish politician who served as President of the European Commission from 2014 to 2019, playing a key role in negotiating the European N Union’s position on Brexit. Discussion The study findings show that users tended to have very similar political values. The results are not necessarily representative of all visitors to the archaeological galleries of the three museums, but rather of those who engaged meaningfully with the intervention. They reveal a rather homogeneous group of visitors, most of whom support the first-wave feminism of the Suffragettes, are pro-European Union, anti-Brexit, critical of imperialism and non-authoritarian (see Section 3.1). Although the case study museums are located in areas with diverse political leanings, the majority of research participants held liberal views. Their mindset appears ARTICLE IN PRESS incompatible with exclusive nationalist thinking that antagonises others based on identity markers such as ethnicity, origin, gender and sexuality, lifestyle, culture and religion. For example, given their overall mostly positive assessment of Boudica and negative evaluations of Theresa May and Margaret Thatcher, visitors who engaged with Tolerant Futures would not view Boudica and Theresa May as similarly heroic figures–a parallel featured in nationalist discourse within social media debates centred on Brexit (Bonacchi, 2022: 104–7). The implications of these results are profound and suggest that bespoke museum-based interventions targeting adults are unlikely to engage people with anti-liberal and intolerant views. Such findings align with Smith’s conclusions (2021) that most–though not all–visitors tend to interact with displays on topics to which they are attuned, given their backgrounds. Our study, however, provides further insights. First, Tolerant Futures leveraged the ancient past, which is often regarded as more distant and, thus, ‘less charged’ than recent history. This was not the case, and the intervention was not better able to carry curatorial messages of social inclusivity and tolerance because of its focus on later prehistory and Roman Britain rather than on events and phenomena within living memory. Second, even the open-ended fSormat of the interactive, designed to ‘provoke’ without instructing visitors about right and wrong answers, proved S ineffective in engaging less liberal individuals. E R Moreover, our research reveals that visitors who interacted with Tolerant Futures had a nuanced, P critical and multifaceted understanding of the Iron Age and Roman past. Participants’ perception of this past as violent is crucial, particularly their awareness of violence in both the Roman and N British empires. In addition, respondents expressed very different views on whether these two I empires were civilised or barbaric, and crude or refined. Overall, such findings show that Tolerant Futures users did not have simpElistic ideas of the Roman and British empires as benevolent bearers of progress and soLphistication that necessarily improved the lives of local peoples. This trope has been used Cto justify power imbalances in nationalist discourse, historically and today (Gardner,I 2017; Hingley, 2019; Bonacchi, 2022). T In recent years, building oRn the tradition of postcolonial archaeology, heritage sites in Britain have embraced a moreA radical ethos centred on highlighting the nature and consequences of imperialism, constraints on mobility, and increasing social inequality (cf. Mills et al., 2013; Eckardt and Müldner, 2016; Mills, 2021). Polm (2016: 239) notes that the Museum of London’s display on Roman Britain shifted to presenting cultural change in London as a ‘process of […] negotiation resulting in the creation of hybrid identities’–a way of characterising transformation that moves away from earlier Romanisation models. The new London Museum, currently under development, will focus further on diversity (Redfern, 2024). As discussed above, such changes have been in step with a wider move by heritage institutions–and Galleries, Libraries, Archives and Museums more generally–towards activist agendas that pursue social inclusion and engage with questions about the appropriateness of being open to any visitors regardless of their political views (Gurian, 2017; ICOM, 2022; Message, 2022). However, it is unclear whether a similar trend has taken place in classrooms. It is not encouraging, for example, that Nagre (2023: 1) found several colonial tropes present in nine history textbooks used in secondary schools in England. These included depictions of “Oriental” others as barbaric, and ideas of native ‘savagery’ and lack of progress. A deeper decolonisation of primary and secondary school curricula may be necessary for more widespread, critical understandings of Roman and British imperialism among future generations (cf. Scott et al., 2023). ARTICLE IN PRESS The results of our beta regression modelling show a clear link between attitudes towards specific pairs of past–present concepts, even though the historical analogies are not the same as those featured in exclusive nationalist discourse. Even among our generally liberal study participants, who held rather sophisticated views of the Iron Age and Roman world, we discovered correlations between perceptions of certain concepts from the IAR past and concepts from modern history and the present. Importantly, we found evidence of these correlations beyond the context of online political activism, as we gathered data through direct questioning in museums. Although we could not demonstrate causal links, this finding does suggest that challenging people’s knowledge of the Iron Age and the Roman world may help change attitudes towards the present. However, the question remains: what interventions could be successfully implemented? By fostering different understandings of the deep past, school education can shape tolerant perceptions of others in the present. Activities organised in partnership with museums can play a key role in this process, since museums are often recognised as auSthoritative sources of information and, as argued by Fishbein (2002: 219–220), ‘authorities can be a major vehicle for S modifying prejudice’. Focusing on children’s and young people’s attitudes might be particularly E productive due to its potential intergenerational impact. Psychological studies show that parents’ R ideological positions often mirror those of their adolescent children regarding right-wing P authoritarianism and social dominance orientation, indicating that ‘generalised prejudice runs in families’ (Meeusen and Dhont, 2015: 585). In addition, peer influence affects adolescents’ levels N of prejudice over time. As children grow up, prejudice is determined more by social factors than I by age and development (Hjerm et al., 2018: 1). For instance, Bobba, Branje and Crocetti (2024: 1522) note that both the ‘family and clasEsroom are important contexts that can contribute to the socialisation of ethnic prejudice’. L C Numerous studies have demonstIrated that parents can act as role models for children, promoting value alignment. However, reTcent research indicates that the effects of socialisation can also work in the opposite direcRtion (Knafo and Galansky, 2008; Benish-Weisman, Levy, and Knafo, 2013; Pedraza and PerAry, 2019; Pagano et al., 2024: 1599). Adolescents, in particular, can influence their parents’ views on topics like pandemic disbelief and COVID-19 vaccination hesitancy (Mantina et al., 2024), immigration (Miklikowska, 2016), and the environment (Damerell, Howe, and Milner-Gulland, 2013; Žukauskienė et al., 2021). Furthermore, the effect of adolescent children’s opinions on the beliefs of their adult parents seems to be particularly significant in relation to issues that are heavily politicised and ideologically charged, such as climate change (Lawson et al., 2018). Therefore, testing the role of historical analogies in fostering tolerance among children, through combined school and museum education programmes, seems a convincing way forward to have an impact not only on future adult generations but also on current ones. 7. Conclusion This study is the first to use a Bayesian framework to quantitatively examine museum visitors’ perceptions of historical analogies and to explore the relationship between their views of the ancient past and their present-day political ideas. The results advance the fields of heritage, ARTICLE IN PRESS museum and memory studies, both methodologically and empirically. They also provide insights of potential interest to cultural sociology and cultural policy scholars, as well as to psychologists working on analogical reasoning. Our research contribution is twofold. First, our findings quantitatively confirm a hypothesis that emerged from qualitative research (Bozoglu, 2019): most adult visitors tend to engage with themes aligned with their political leanings. This adds to observations that visitors prefer displays to which they feel attuned, given their social and demographic backgrounds (e.g., Smith, 2021). Our results show that those who engage with on- site interventions that promote tolerance by challenging divisive historical analogies tend to already hold liberal and non-authoritarian views. Furthermore, this group demonstrates a critical understanding of politically charged historical concepts relating to imperialism and heroic figures often featured in stereotyped ways within exclusive nationalist discourse (Bonacchi, 2022). Second, through predictive modelling, we found correlations between specific pairs of past–present concepts, suggesting the potential to influence attitudes towards others–and tolerance–via people’s perceptions of historical analogies. We conclude, therefore, that museums, as heritage sites, have limited potential to attract, engagSe–and, thus, change–the attitudes of adults with non-liberal and more authoritarian mindsets, even when they employ S interventions focused on the distant rather than the recent past and designed with an open-ended E format. However, they can play a vital role, in partnership with school educators, in promoting R tolerance among children by fostering nuanced and critical interpretations of the ancient past. We P propose that this is the most promising route to intergenerational attitude change. JSON: Name: tolerant_futures_pipeline Title: Randomized field experiment and Bayesian hierarchical beta-regression pipeline to evaluate the causal impact of an interactive museum intervention on visitors' tolerance and historical-analogy alignment Short Hypothesis: Randomized exposure to an interactive museum intervention that exposes and challenges binary historical analogies causes an immediate and sustained increase in measured tolerance among child visitors (ages 8–16) but not among adult visitors (ages 18+). Related Work: Existing work comprises observational and qualitative museum evaluations, cross-sectional surveys of visitor demographics, and correlational analyses linking historical narratives to political attitudes. Prior interventions are typically single-site, non-randomized, or rely on qualitative interpretation; quantitative analyses have used standard regressions without fully modeling bounded analogue-placement data or hierarchical dependence across visitors, concepts, and sites. Limitations of current approaches include selection bias from self-selected museum audiences, absence of randomized controls for causal inference, coarse treatment of spectrum data (ignoring boundary constraints and multimodality), limited treatment of children as a distinct target population, small or convenience samples, and minimal use of hierarchical Bayesian methods that jointly model item-level analogies, individual heterogeneity, and site effects. No prior pipeline combines randomized deployment, pre-post-follow-up measurement across age cohorts, and Bayesian beta-regression of analogue placements with explicit ablations isolating interaction components. Abstract: Problem: Museums aim to foster tolerance by challenging binary historical analogies, but existing evidence is correlational and focused on adult visitors. Approach: We propose a mixed-method pipeline combining randomized field deployment of an interactive exhibit, age-stratified pre/post/follow-up surveys, and hierarchical Bayesian beta-regression to model visitors' analogue-placement data and changes in tolerance. Main contribution: The pipeline enables causal estimation of intervention effects on tolerance for children versus adults, models analogue-placement data bounded on [0,1] with concept-specific slopes and participant- and site-level random effects, and evaluates which interactive components (open text, intergroup exposure, spectra framing) drive any observed changes via randomized ablation arms. Expected outcome: The pipeline will quantify immediate and sustained changes in tolerance and shifts in historical-analogy alignment, produce posterior estimates and predictive checks for generalization across sites, and identify which interaction elements produce the largest measurable effects in child audiences. Experiments: Overview: Pre-register an age-stratified randomized controlled trial across three archaeological museums and partner schools; implement three arms: (A) full interactive (Tolerant Futures), (B) UI-matched neutral control interactive (same mechanics, non-political historical content), (C) no-interactive control (standard visit). Datasets: (1) New field dataset: N_total=2400 participants across sites: 3 museums × 2 cohorts (children 8–16, adults 18+) × target n=400 per cohort per site aggregated to 2400; (2) school-group cohort: N_schools=24 classes, ~25 pupils/class; (3) existing Tolerant Futures dataset (Zenodo) for baseline replication. Collected variables: analogue placements (continuous in [0,1]) for each past–present pair, free-text rationales, pre/post/follow-up tolerance scale (3-dimensional acceptance/respect/appreciation), RWA (right-wing authoritarianism) and SDO scales, political ideology, socio-demographics, attendance mode (school vs casual visitor), and parent-report for children. Timeline: pre-visit survey (baseline), immediate post-intervention survey, 3-month follow-up survey. Baselines for comparisons: (i) neutral interactive vs full interactive, (ii) full interactive vs no-interactive visit, (iii) adult vs child cohorts. Analytical models: primary model is hierarchical Bayesian beta regression predicting present-day analogue scores using participant-level past-scores, concept-pair specific intercepts and slopes, random intercepts for participant and museum, and arm-by-cohort interaction terms; priors weakly informative. Evaluation metrics: primary outcome = change in tolerance score (post minus pre) with posterior credible intervals; secondary outcomes = change in alignment coefficient (slope of past→present), proportion shifting across pre-defined tolerance thresholds, Bayes factors for null vs alternative, WAIC/LOO for model comparison, posterior predictive checks, effect-size (Cohen's d equivalents from posterior). Ablation studies: randomized sub-arms within full interactive that (1) remove free-text explanation, (2) remove exposure-to-other-visitor choices (no Chapter 3), (3) reduce spectrum complexity (fewer adjectives). Sensitivity analyses: model fit with zero-and-one-inflated beta, alternative link functions, covariate adjustment, and per-site stratified models. Implementation details: MCMC settings: 4 chains, 4000 iterations, 1000 warmup; convergence criteria Rhat<1.01; pre-registered thresholds for practical significance (e.g., posterior probability >95% that delta_tolerance > 0.1 SD). Risk Factors and Limitations: Selection bias: participants who choose to use an interactive are non-random even within randomized arms; school cohorts may differ from casual visitors. Social desirability and demand characteristics: explicit tolerance questions and on-site research may induce response bias. Measurement issues: analogue placements at exact 0 or 1 create boundary mass that can violate pure beta assumptions, necessitating zero-one-inflated models. Attrition: follow-up loss, especially among adults, can bias longitudinal estimates. Small effect sizes: required sample sizes may be larger than planned, reducing power. Ethical and consent constraints: child recruitment requires parental consent and may limit demographic reach. Generalizability: findings may not transfer beyond archaeological galleries, the UK cultural context, or to different historical topics. Modeling risks: hierarchical Bayesian models can be computationally intensive and sensitive to prior choices and model mis-specification. Text-analysis risks: free-text rationales may be noisy, short, and culturally biased, complicating automated sentiment or topic modeling. Intervention contamination: visitors in no-interactive control may be exposed indirectly to intervention content in shared galleries. Regulatory/logistical constraints: museum schedules, device availability, and staffing can limit randomized assignment fidelity.
